Its two strong modules with several nodes are tinted: A, B, C, D in the accent color and F, G, H in teal. Right: the decomposition tree. The prime root M1 has four children: the series module M2 (accent) over A, B, C, D, the leaf E, the parallel module M3 (teal) over F, G, H, and the leaf I." width="100%"} A *module* is a set of nodes that every outside node treats alike: it is adjacent to all of them or to none. Modules are the parts of a graph that can be collapsed to a single node without losing information, much as a group of interchangeable members acts as one unit to the rest of a network. The *strong* modules, those that overlap no other module, nest into a single tree, the modular decomposition, which describes every module of the graph. Each tree node is a strong module. Its leaves are the single nodes of the graph, and each internal node has one of three types, chosen by how its children connect: - `"parallel"`: the module is disconnected, and its children are its components. - `"series"`: the complement of the module is disconnected, so every child is joined to every other, and its children are the complement's components. - `"prime"`: neither, and its children are its maximal proper modules. Collapsing them leaves a graph with no modules other than single nodes and the whole graph. The result is a new directed graph with an edge from each module to each of its children. Leaves keep the labels of the nodes they hold and internal nodes are labeled `"M1"`, `"M2"`, ... in preorder, so `"M1"` is the root unless the graph has a single node (then the tree is that one leaf). If some node of the graph is already labeled like that, the prefix is doubled (`"MM1"`, ...) until the labels are distinct. Every tree node has a `type` attribute (`"parallel"`, `"series"`, `"prime"` or `"leaf"`) and a `nodes` attribute listing the labels of the original nodes in the module. Children appear in the order of their smallest node ID. Self-loops and parallel edges are ignored. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A new directed, unweighted graph holding the decomposition tree. The empty graph gives an empty tree. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the graph is directed. ::: ## See Also {.doc-see-also} [](`~is_cograph`) : Whether the tree has no prime nodes. ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} NetworkX pull request #7957 (not yet merged) ports an existing C++ implementation; this one is written independently from the definitions. A module that is disconnected, or whose complement is, splits into the components (found in $O(V + E)$ time, or by a complement search over the unvisited nodes). Otherwise the module is prime, and its children come from the vertex partitioning of Ehrenfeucht et al. (1994): partition refinement from a pivot node $v$ splits the other nodes into the maximal modules that avoid $v$, in time linear in their edges, and a forcing digraph on those parts (part $X$ forces $Y$ when $Y$ tells $X$ apart from $v$) has a unique source component made of the parts outside the largest proper module holding $v$. The children are those parts plus that module. The tree is unique, so the result is the same as NetworkX's (which reports the root separately and accepts a pivot picker that cannot change the answer). Each level costs near-linear time for sparse modules; deep trees on dense graphs, such as threshold graphs, approach $O(V^3)$. ## Examples {.doc-examples} Four friends A to D all know one another, and E knows them all, along with F, G and H, who don't know each other but all know I: ::: {#8925a58c .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec g = ec.Graph().add_nodes(list("ABCDEFGHI")) g.add_edges([(a, b) for a in "ABCD" for b in "ABCDE" if a < b]) g.add_edges([("E", x) for x in "FGH"] + [(x, "I") for x in "FGH"]) tree = g.modular_decomposition() { tree.get_label_from_id(n): (attrs["type"], attrs["nodes"]) for n in sorted(tree.get_node_ids(limit=None)) if (attrs := tree.get_node(n).attributes)["type"] != "leaf" } ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` {'M1': ('prime', ['A', 'B', 'C', 'D', 'E', 'F', 'G', 'H', 'I']), 'M2': ('series', ['A', 'B', 'C', 'D']), 'M3': ('parallel', ['F', 'G', 'H'])} ``` ::: ::: The clique A to D is a series module and F, G, H a parallel one; with E and I they are the children of the prime root: ::: {#088afffb .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} tree.get_edges_str_repr(use_labels=True) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` ['M1->M2', 'M2->A', 'M2->B', 'M2->C', 'M2->D', 'M1->E', 'M1->M3', 'M3->F', 'M3->G', 'M3->H', 'M1->I'] ``` ::: :::
